transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-20 15:00 PST | Duration: 54m | Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Gupta (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Singh (Evergreen), Carlos Ruiz (Evergreen Eng), Priya Patel (Evergreen Security), Evan Moore (Evergreen PM)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, happy holidays almost — we'll keep this tight. Quick intro, i'm lena, AE, and ravi's our solutions engineer. We want to nail down success criteria and the quality eval plan for the POC.

[00:18] Dr. Maya Singh: Thanks Lena. We're primarily focused on an assistant to support clinical documentation triage — so quality is top priority, low hallucination, strict format compliance. We have about 1.5k daily user interactions, peak qps around 6, avg payload 150-250 tokens.

[00:34] Ravi Gupta: Got it. For the POC we usually do: 1) baseline with hosted API, 2) run dedicated harness with our bench scripts, and 3) quality eval using golden prompts + regression tests. Quick question — do you have any existing golden responses or a rubric?

[00:49] Dr. Maya Singh: We have a small gold set — maybe 50 canonical responses for critical paths. We'll expand to 200 for the pilot. Concern is throughput and latency: clinicians expect sub-800ms p95 for short prompts.

[01:05] Carlos Ruiz: Also want to evaluate cost per 1k tokens at scale; that's a gating factor for long-term. We'll compare hosted vs dedicated pricing.

[01:17] Lena Park: Makes sense. For quality eval plan — propose the following: golden prompt set (200 prompts, 50 high-stakes golden responses), automatic regression suite (runners that check exact-match and fuzzy-match scores), hallucination detector (entity hallucination checks and fact-consistency heuristics), format/structure checks (JSON schema validation for structured outputs), and a scoring approach that combines precision, recall for entities, and a human review sample.

[01:43] Priya Patel: On security, we need SOC2 report, network diagram, and confirmation we can use customer KMS for key management if we use Private deployment. Also SSO/SAML support.

[01:55] Ravi Gupta: Yep, we'll send SOC2 + ISO docs. For Private we support customer-managed KMS; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and can bring-your-own-key on Dedicated/Private. SSO is supported — SAML and OIDC.

[02:12] Evan Moore: Timeline? We're hoping to show results to stakeholders in mid-Jan. Is that realistic?

[02:20] Lena Park: Realistic. Proposed timeline: week 0 (this week) - agree eval plan + sign pilot; week 1 - infra setup & dataset ingestion; week 2 - benchmark runs and initial quality eval; week 3 - analysis and human review, stakeholder demo end of week 3. So roughly 3 weeks from kickoff to demo.

[02:41] Dr. Maya Singh: That aligns. A few clarifying items on scoring: do you have a recommended scoring formula?

[02:49] Ravi Gupta: We typically compute composite score = 0.5 * automated quality score + 0.3 * latency compliance score + 0.2 * human judgement. Automated quality score is weighted between exact-match (30%), semantic similarity (40%), entity correctness (30%). For hallucination we run an entity hallucination rate and flag anything over 1% for critical prompts.

[03:15] Carlos Ruiz: For responses that must follow strict JSON schema, how do you measure format compliance?

[03:21] Ravi Gupta: We run JSON schema validation; we report % valid. For partial failures we extract meaningful error messages and include example failure cases in the report. We also run a recovery policy test — e.g., with function/tool calling turned on, see if model adheres to tool response format.

[03:40] Dr. Maya Singh: And hallucination checks — can you detect when the model invents a medication or a diagnosis? That's our biggest fear.

[03:48] Ravi Gupta: We do NER-based checks versus the input context and a curated medical knowledge baseline; full-proof detection is hard, so we also recommend human sampling of top 200 high-risk generations. Also include negative prompts and adversarial test cases in regression.

[04:04] Priya Patel: Network wise, if we go Private, our infra team wants a VPC peering or private link and an on-prem agent — is that supported?

[04:12] Lena Park: Yes, Private supports VPC peering and an optional on-prem package. We'll include the network diagram and egress requirements in the infra checklist.

[04:23] Evan Moore: For benchmarks, what does the harness output look like? Latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens?

[04:30] Ravi Gupta: Exactly. Our harness will produce latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99), throughput graphs, GPU utilization, and estimated cost per 1M tokens under different quantization profiles. We'll also share trace logs for failed requests.

[04:45] Dr. Maya Singh: Do you recommend quantized models for clinical text? Concern about quality regressions.

[04:51] Ravi Gupta: We recommend starting with 8-bit or 4-bit LLMs but always run the quality eval in the loop. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles by workload; we'll include that as part of the POC analysis. If you have critical prompts, we keep those on full-precision variants as a fallback.

[05:08] Carlos Ruiz: On dataset size and workload sizing — we will provide 10k historical notes redacted and a production-like stream of 1.5k daily. For bench we can simulate 100 concurrent sessions to recreate peaks.

[05:20] Lena Park: Perfect. For golden prompts, please prioritize 50 critical clinical flows (prescriptions, discharge summaries, alerts). We'll use those for exact-match and hallucination checks.

[05:30] Dr. Maya Singh: What's an acceptable pass threshold?

[05:33] Ravi Gupta: For critical flows I'd recommend >= 95% format compliance, <= 1% critical hallucination rate, p95 latency < 800ms on hosted or <400ms on Dedicated (depending on region), and composite quality score > 0.85. These are starting points we can tune.

[05:52] Priya Patel: We'll need to add legal acceptance criteria for PHI handling and retention — can you confirm retention defaults?

[05:59] Lena Park: By default hosted retains logs for 30 days; Dedicated/Private can be configured to zero retention. We'll send the retention policy and options.

[06:07] Carlos Ruiz: A quick note on benchmarking: include end-to-end latency (client->model->client) and tokenization overhead, because our client code does heavy preprocessing.

[06:16] Ravi Gupta: We'll capture end-to-end traces. Also include KV cache hit-rate metrics for long conversations.

[06:26] Dr. Maya Singh: For regression tests, can you include adversarial prompts that try to elicit hallucinations?

[06:31] Ravi Gupta: Yes — adversarial prompt suite will be part of the regression. We'll run before/after comparisons for each model variant and quantization setting.

[06:40] Evan Moore: Anything about cost controls during pilot? We want budget caps.

[06:44] Lena Park: We'll put rate limits and daily caps; Redwood Console can enforce quotas and send alerts if thresholds are hit.

[06:52] Dr. Maya Singh: Ok, last thing — human review. What's the sample size?

[06:56] Ravi Gupta: We recommend 300 random samples and 200 targeted high-risk samples for human review. Reviews will be done by your clinical SMEs and we'll provide an annotation template.

[07:08] Lena Park: Great, to recap: Redwood will share eval template, infra checklist, SOC2 + network diagram, and pricing/pilot agreement. Evergreen will share sample prompts/responses, stand up sandbox, and confirm security requirements. We'll schedule the benchmark run for week of 2026-12-29 and aim to have a stakeholder demo by week of 2027-01-18.

[07:29] Dr. Maya Singh: Sounds good. Thanks, team.

[07:33] Carlos Ruiz: Thanks. We'll review and get the artifacts over.

[07:36] Priya Patel: I'll look into KMS requirements and circle back.

[07:40] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc pack.

End of transcript

References/links mentioned in call: - Redwood quality-eval-template (link to be sent) - Benchmark harness repo (link) - Redwood SOC2 + security pack (link)
